topics.title: AI Is Running Out of Text
topics.topic: the data wall in AI training
topics.angle: why high-quality text is becoming the bottleneck
topics.hook: AI companies spent years chasing more compute. The next shortage is stranger: readable text.

beats.text: Large models are trained on trillions of words scraped from the open web, books, code and subtitles.
beats.headline: Trillions of words

beats.text: That pool is finite, and the best quality slice of it is smaller than most people assume.
beats.headline: A finite pool

beats.text: Publishers are restricting crawlers, and licensed archives cost real money, so fresh supply is tightening.
beats.headline: Supply tightening

beats.text: The workaround is synthetic data, human feedback or smaller models trained on cleaner, curated text.
beats.headline: Three workarounds

topics.payoff: The winners may not be the labs with the most data, but the ones with the cleanest way to replace it.
topics.cta: Follow for more on how AI actually gets built.

topics.title: The AI Moving Onto Your Phone
topics.angle: why small local models are suddenly competitive
topics.hook: The most useful AI of the next few years may never leave your phone.

beats.text: Running a model on-device removes network latency, cloud bills and most privacy questions in one move.
beats.headline: Three problems gone

beats.text: Quantisation and distillation shrink models to a few billion parameters without destroying everyday reasoning.
beats.headline: Smaller, not dumber

beats.text: Phone chips now ship dedicated neural hardware measured in tens of trillions of operations per second.
beats.headline: Neural silicon

beats.text: The catch is memory bandwidth and battery, which is why tiny models still beat big ones on a handset.
beats.headline: The catch

topics.payoff: Expect hybrids: a small model handling the everyday work, and the cloud called only for the hard questions.
topics.cta: Follow for more on where AI is heading.

topics.title: AI's Real Limit Is Electricity
topics.angle: why power, not chips, constrains AI growth
topics.hook: A GPU you cannot power is a very expensive paperweight.

beats.text: Training and serving large models turns electricity into answers, and demand is climbing fast.
beats.headline: Electricity in, answers out

beats.text: Grid connections, transformers and cooling now take longer to secure than the servers themselves.
beats.headline: The slow part

beats.text: That is pushing operators toward dedicated power contracts, on-site generation and colder climates.
beats.headline: New siting rules

beats.text: Efficiency work, from better chips to smarter batching, quietly decides who can afford to scale.
beats.headline: Efficiency is strategy

topics.payoff: Watch the power purchase agreements, not the benchmark charts. They predict the next model release.
topics.cta: Follow for more on the systems behind AI.

topics.title: Robots Learn by Watching Video
topics.angle: how internet video becomes robot skill
topics.hook: Robots used to need demonstrations. Now they are learning from videos anyone can record.

beats.text: A robot arm needs thousands of examples to learn one grasp, and human demonstrations are slow and costly.
beats.headline: The data problem

beats.text: Video pretraining lets a model watch ordinary footage first and infer how objects move and get held.
beats.headline: Pretrain on video

beats.text: The gap is action: a video shows what happened, not the exact forces a hand applied to make it happen.
beats.headline: Seeing is not doing

beats.text: The fix is a small amount of real robot data to anchor the model, then scale with cheap footage.
beats.headline: Anchor, then scale

topics.payoff: The future of robot training looks less like programming and more like a very large video library.
topics.cta: Follow for more on AI in the physical world.

topics.title: Open Weights Are Catching Up
topics.angle: the shrinking gap between open and closed models
topics.hook: The gap between the best closed model and the best free one is now measured in months.

beats.text: Open weight releases publish the trained parameters, so anyone can run, fine-tune or inspect the model.
beats.headline: What open weights means

beats.text: Each strong closed release is followed by open models that reach similar scores a few months later.
beats.headline: A shrinking lag

beats.text: Teams pick open weights when they need privacy, offline use, or a model they can specialise cheaply.
beats.headline: Why teams switch

beats.text: The trade-off is support, safety tooling and the engineering cost of running inference yourself.
beats.headline: The trade-off

topics.payoff: Open weights turn the model into a commodity. The product advantage moves to data and workflow.
topics.cta: Follow for more on the AI stack.

topics.title: Nobody Knows If AI Works
topics.hook: A benchmark score can be misleading when test answers leak into training data.

beats.text: Public test sets can appear online and may be included in later training data.
beats.headline: Contamination

beats.text: A model may memorize familiar examples yet struggle with new questions that test the same skill.
beats.headline: Memorised, not learned

beats.text: Private or newly written tests can reduce some leakage risk, while differences between test sets can make comparisons harder.
beats.headline: Private tests

beats.text: Use public leaderboards for broad comparisons, then test candidates on representative, held-out examples from your own workload.
beats.headline: Measure your task

topics.payoff: Treat leaderboards as a starting point, then check shortlisted models on held-out examples from your workload.
topics.cta: Follow for more sober AI coverage.
